questions.a: The supporting character is the farmer described as "g^s&d^s tkV" (an old weather-beaten peasant) who says "Hkkjr ekrk ls mudk eryc èkjrh ls gS" (Bharat Mata's meaning comes from the land). A wrong answer (e.g., naming Nehru himself or a generic "villager") reveals the student cannot distinguish the protagonist from supporting characters or cannot recall specific textual details about who speaks which line.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why Nehru includes the voices of ordinary villagers and a farmer when exploring the meaning of "Bharat Mata" instead of only presenting his own intellectual analysis.
questions.a: Nehru includes these voices to demonstrate that the idea of India lives in the lived experience of its people, not just in abstract theory - the farmer's answer "from the land" grounds the concept in material reality, while the villagers' initial confusion shows the gap between nationalist rhetoric and popular understanding. A wrong answer focusing only on "making the essay interesting" or "showing diversity" misses the structural purpose: these characters embody the thesis that India is its people.

questions.q: Compare how the farmer's definition of Bharat Mata ("from the land") differs from the urban intellectual's likely definition, and analyze what this contrast reveals about Nehru's view of nationalism.
questions.a: The farmer defines Bharat Mata materially (land, soil, sustenance) while an intellectual would likely define it abstractly (culture, history, civilization). This contrast reveals Nehru's view that true nationalism must bridge both - the emotional-intellectual idea must be rooted in the material reality of the masses. A wrong answer treating both definitions as "equally valid perspectives" misses Nehru's synthesis: he values the farmer's definition as more authentic because it comes from lived struggle.

questions.q: Evaluate whether the supporting characters in "Hkkjr ekrk" have distinct individual personalities or function primarily as collective voices. Defend your judgment with textual evidence.
questions.a: They function primarily as collective voices - the farmer is unnamed ("g^s&d^s tkV"), villagers speak in chorus ("os ,d&nwljs dh rjI+kQ ;k esjh rjI+kQ ns[kus yx tkrs"), and Nehru generalizes ("bu yksxksa dh t;"). Only the farmer gets a specific line, but even he represents a type (peasant). This serves Nehru's purpose: the "character" of India is collective. A wrong answer claiming they are "well-developed characters" imposes fictional expectations on a non-fiction essay.

questions.q: Write a 4-line dialogue between Nehru and a NEW supporting character (e.g., a young woman weaver from Banaras) that would fit seamlessly into the chapter, revealing a dimension of Bharat Mata not yet expressed.
questions.a: A strong answer creates a voice that adds a new dimension (e.g., women's labor, artistic heritage, intergenerational memory) while matching Nehru's respectful tone and the chapter's theme of unity-in-diversity. Example: "Didi, Bharat Mata is the thread my grandmother spun, the sari I weave, the hunger in my fingers - and the hope that my daughter's loom will sing freer songs." A poor answer creates a character who merely repeats existing perspectives or speaks in anachronistic modern vocabulary.
